prohibited_recommendations: Do not give corticosteroids as monotherapy in GBS.
Do not start plasma exchange without considering coagulation status given PBC.
required_recommendations: Initiate IVIG 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days; verify hepatic synthetic function (coagulation, albumin) prior to treatment.
Document baseline liver function and avoid hepatotoxic adjuncts.
Coordinate care with hepatology for PBC comanagement.

avoided_actions.rationale: GBS is a peripheral nerve / nerve-root disorder; EEG has no role in diagnosis unless atypical CNS features (encephalopathy, seizures) are present.
Echocardiography is not indicated in typical GBS; reserve for pre-existing cardiac disease or unexplained hemodynamic instability after autonomic causes are excluded.
Head CT contributes no diagnostic information in GBS; the disease is peripheral and CT does not visualise nerve roots reliably.
Brain MRI is reserved for atypical features (encephalopathy, CNS signs, transverse myelitis on differential). In classic GBS it does not aid diagnosis.

accepted: Guillain-Barré syndrome, AIDP (post-bronchitis), with concurrent PBC-associated immunologic background

differential.key_features: Primary biliary cholangitis can be associated with cryoglobulinaemia and vasculitic neuropathy — typically asymmetric mononeuropathy multiplex, not symmetric ascending areflexic weakness.
Time course at presentation is too short to discriminate; revisit beyond 8 weeks.
Encephalopathic features absent; bilirubin / ammonia not consistent.
UDCA is not a recognised cause of acute polyradiculoneuropathy.

key_clinical_evidence: Coexisting autoimmune liver disease may complicate workup but does not change the GBS diagnostic threshold.
Vasculitic neuropathy associated with autoimmune comorbidities is typically asymmetric, distinguishing it from symmetric GBS.
Treatment choice between IVIG and PLEX should incorporate hepatic synthetic and coagulation status.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: PBC-associated neuropathy is typically asymmetric and chronic; the symmetric, ascending, areflexic, albuminocytologic-dissociation profile is GBS.
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchor on a vasculitic or autoimmune neuropathy specific to PBC.

sequence_constraints.reason: Document respiratory status (FVC/NIF) before committing to IVIG vs plasma exchange — severe respiratory compromise mandates ICU triage and may influence treatment choice and timing.
Renal function, IgA screen, and CBC must be reviewed before IVIG to mitigate renal failure, anaphylaxis (IgA-deficient patients), and aseptic meningitis risk.

specialized_test.impression: This is an ABNORMAL nerve conduction study. 1. Prolonged distal motor latencies and reduced conduction velocities in bilateral peroneal and tibial motor nerves, with reduced CMAP amplitudes; borderline changes in median motor nerves. 2. Absent sural sensory nerve action potentials bilaterally. 3. Absent F-waves bilaterally (peroneal); prolonged F-wave latency in bilateral median nerves (56 ms). 4. Absent H-reflex bilaterally. 5. EMG: neurogenic motor unit changes in lower extremity muscles; short-duration polyphasic units in proximal muscles also noted. Demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with proximal involvement. Mixed neurogenic and possible myopathic EMG features

quantitative_data.pattern: Mixed demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy with concurrent myopathic features on EMG

metadata.difficulty_description: Elevated CK and myoglobin with PBC background and statin use — multiple competing diagnoses for proximal weakness; NCS pattern is decisive

patient.chief_complaint: Six-week progressive weakness predominantly proximal lower extremities, preceded by bronchitis, with absent knee and ankle reflexes.

family_history: No relevant family history of neuromuscular disease
past_medical_history: Primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), end-stage liver disease, Child-Pugh B

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. V. is a 54-year-old woman with end-stage liver disease secondary to primary biliary cholangitis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and remote splenectomy presenting with a 6-week history of progressive weakness. She had an episode of bronchitis approximately 7 weeks ago requiring a short course of antibiotics. One week after the bronchitis resolved, she began noticing difficulty rising from a chair and climbing stairs. The weakness has been primarily proximal and lower extremity-predominant. She denies any sensory symptoms, pain, or difficulty with sphincters. She has no diplopia or dysphagia. She denies alcohol use. Her atorvastatin was continued throughout. Her husband noted she seemed more confused than her baseline mild hepatic encephalopathy, though ammonia is not significantly elevated. The 6-week duration of proximal weakness, together with the statin use, liver disease, and elevated muscle enzymes, raised initial concern for an inflammatory or statin-induced myopathy or a chronic demyelinating polyneuropathy.

neurological_exam.additional: FVC: 1.8 L (predicted 2.9 L — 62%). NIF: -28 cmH2O. Serum CK markedly elevated on admission. Proximal > distal weakness pattern. History of 6 weeks of progressive weakness, with onset following bronchitis.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact finger-nose bilaterally. Limited heel-shin assessment.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Intact. No facial weakness. No ophthalmoplegia. Gag preserved.
neurological_exam.gait: Unable to assess — patient cannot stand.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented. Mildly encephalopathic at baseline (known hepatic encephalopathy grade 1).
neurological_exam.motor: Proximal lower extremity weakness: hip flexion 3/5 bilaterally, knee extension 3+/5. Upper extremity proximal strength 4/5. Distal strength 4+/5.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Absent bilateral patellar and Achilles. Trace bilateral biceps. Downgoing plantars.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact light touch and pinprick throughout.
